summary.text: 没 is the standardized simplified form of 沒, whose received dictionary gloss is “sink” or “submerge.” Its common reading méi means “not have”; the graph may have been reused for this different word because the words may have sounded alike, though the older word’s sound and the proposed match remain uncertain.

formation.text: The traditional graph’s construction is disputed. The received 說文 analysis has 水 plus 𠬸; later commentary treats 𠬸 as a sound element, while another account describes a hand reaching into water. These accounts do not settle the graph’s original construction, and the historical sound relation of 𠬸 to 沒 remains unverified.

history.text: 没 is identified as the standardized simplified form of 沒 and is also classified as a variant. A variant-dictionary account says the right side of a common form was corrupted into 殳; this does not establish a complete graphic sequence leading to standardized 没. The related form 𣳚 is described as stroke-reduced, but its cited inscription is undated and does not establish such a sequence.

uncertainties.text: The hand-in-water picture and the analysis of 沒 as 水 plus 𠬸 are competing explanations; the original construction remains unsettled.
Later commentary assigns 𠬸 a sound role, but its reading and historical sound relation to 沒 remain unverified.

The origin and chronology of méi “not have” remain unresolved. One proposal is that 沒, used for “sink” or “drown,” was reused to write the different word “not have” because the words may have sounded alike; the older word’s sound and the proposed match are unverified. Other proposals involve 勿, 未, or 有.

senses.text: The received 說文 glosses 沒 as 沈, “sink” or “submerge”; dictionary accounts also record sinking and drowning. The use is documented, but its earliest attestation and the graph’s original meaning are not established.
Historical commentary cites uses of 沒 meaning “end” or “exhausted”; the earliest attestation of this sense is unresolved.

In the common reading méi, 沒 is used for “not have” and “none.” One proposal is that the graph used for “sink” or “drown” was reused to write this different word because the words may have sounded alike. The older word’s sound, the proposed match, the borrowing path, and the first use remain unresolved.

limitations.text: The cited examples for “sink” and “end/exhausted” were not independently dated, so the earliest attestations of these senses remain unresolved.
No primary textual evidence establishes the first use of méi “not have” or the proposed sound-based borrowing path.

overview.text: 没 is the simplified form of 沒, commonly read méi and meaning “not have.” The traditional graph is analyzed as water plus a disputed element or as a hand reaching into water; its construction remains unresolved.

takeaway.text: The proposed borrowing explains “not have” as a different word written with 沒 because the words may have sounded alike; that sound match remains uncertain.

relationships.text: 没 is identified as the standardized simplified form of 沒. A separate account describes corruption of the right side in a common variant, but does not establish a complete graphic sequence for standardized 没.
